name.text: Matrix from an object and its image

questiontext.text:
A transformation with matrix \(M\) maps \(P({@Pp[1]@},\,{@Pp[2]@})\) onto \(P'({@Pi[1]@},\,{@Pi[2]@})\) and \(Q({@Qp[1]@},\,{@Qp[2]@})\) onto \(Q'({@Qi[1]@},\,{@Qi[2]@})\).

Find \(M\).

\(M = \) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Method 1 (equations). Let \(M = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\). The top row of \(M\) gives the x-coordinates of the images:

\({@e1@}\) and \({@e2@}\), so \(a = {@ta[1,1]@}\) and \(b = {@ta[1,2]@}\).

The bottom row gives the y-coordinates: \({@e3@}\) and \({@e4@}\), so \(c = {@ta[2,1]@}\) and \(d = {@ta[2,2]@}\).

Method 2 (inverse). Write P and Q as the columns of the object matrix and \(P'\), \(Q'\) as the columns of the image matrix. Then \(M \times\) (object matrix) = (image matrix), so \(M\) = (image matrix) \(\times\) (object matrix)\(^{-1}\):

\(M = {@Im@}{@iO@} = {@ta@}\).

Check: \({@ta@}{@transpose(matrix(Pp))@} = {@transpose(matrix(Pi))@}\).

questiondescription.text:
Matrices and Transformations: matrix from an object and its image

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.1: Find the matrix of a transformation from two points and their images, by equations or with an inverse matrix.

Core

truefeedback.text: Check your matrix on P: it sends P to \(({@aP[1]@},\,{@aP[2]@})\), not to \(P'\). Each row of \(M\) produces one coordinate: the top row gives \(x'\), so its two numbers come from the \(x'\) equations.
That matrix sends \(P'\) back to P: it undoes the transformation. You need the matrix that sends the object to the image.

node.description: Object inverse on the wrong side

truefeedback.text: Since \(M \times\) (object matrix) = (image matrix), multiply by the inverse of the object matrix on the right: \(M\) = (image matrix) \(\times\) (object matrix)\(^{-1}\).

falsefeedback.text:
Your matrix sends P to \(({@aP[1]@},\,{@aP[2]@})\) and Q to \(({@aQ[1]@},\,{@aQ[2]@})\), not to \(P'\) and \(Q'\).

Let \(M = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\). \(M\) times P = \(P'\) gives two equations and \(M\) times Q = \(Q'\) gives two more. Solve for a and b from the \(x'\) equations, and for c and d from the \(y'\) equations.
